claims.claim: A clause is a group of words with a subject and a predicate; an independent clause can stand alone as a complete sentence, while a dependent clause also has a subject and a predicate but cannot stand alone.

The four sentence forms are defined by clause combinations: a simple sentence has one independent clause, a compound sentence has two or more independent clauses, a complex sentence has one independent clause plus at least one dependent clause, and a compound-complex sentence has two or more independent clauses plus at least one dependent clause.
English declarative sentences follow subject-verb-object word order by default, with modifiers and phrases arranged around that core.
Coordinating conjunctions (and, but, for, or, nor, so, yet, remembered as FANBOYS) join two independent clauses in a compound sentence; in formal writing a comma precedes the conjunction.

Subordinating conjunctions such as after, as, before, once, since, until, and while, and relative pronouns such as who, which, and that, introduce dependent clauses, which must attach to an independent clause.

A sentence fragment is an incomplete sentence, usually a piece missing a subject or a predicate or a dependent clause left to stand alone; the fix is to attach it to a nearby clause or supply the missing part.

A run-on (fused sentence) joins two independent clauses with no punctuation at all, and a comma splice joins them with only a comma; the standard fixes are to split them into separate sentences, add a comma plus a coordinating conjunction, or join them with a semicolon.
Varying sentence length and structure improves readability; skilled writers mix short simple sentences for emphasis with compound and complex sentences to show how ideas relate.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether a comma is always required before a coordinating conjunction that joins two short independent clauses.
positions: Formal writing guidance teaches the comma-before-conjunction pattern as the default for joining independent clauses.
In informal writing, short independent clauses are often joined without the comma.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the comma-plus-conjunction pattern as the standard formal convention, which is the pattern the sources present, and notes that writers also choose sentence structure for rhythm and emphasis.

sourceRecords.title: Purdue OWL — Independent and Dependent Clauses
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Defines independent and dependent clauses; dependent clauses are introduced by subordinating conjunctions (after, as, before, once, since, until, while, among others) or relative pronouns (who, whom, whose, which, that) and cannot stand alone. Supports the clause-type claims and the dependent-clause connectors. Reference only; prose synthesized.

sourceRecords.title: Purdue OWL — Run-ons, Comma Splices, and Fused Sentences
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Defines run-ons (fused sentences) and comma splices and presents the standard fixes: split into separate sentences, add a comma plus a coordinating conjunction, or join with a semicolon. Names the coordinating conjunctions (and, but, for, or, nor, so, yet). Supports the FANBOYS claim and the run-on and comma-splice fixes. Reference only.

sourceRecords.title: Purdue OWL — Sentence Fragments
sourceRecords.notes: Verified live on 2026-08-21: 'Fragments are incomplete sentences. Usually, fragments are pieces of sentences that have become disconnected from the main clause.' Supports the claim that recognizing subjects and predicates helps diagnose incomplete sentences.

sourceRecords.title: Language Foundations Handbook — Sentences: Sentence Forms
sourceRecords.notes: Verified live on 2026-08-21: 'In a clause, the subject is the noun or pronoun that is "doing" the verb' and 'a clause is a group of words with a subject and a predicate.' Its compound-sentence example ('He is stretching and he is grooming himself') illustrates coordinated verb phrases, used to support the compound predicate concept. License not stated on the page; treated as reference-only.
